passages.original: ita doctores Ecclesiæ multa verba Evangelii ill cordibus suis congregant, quorum cum obscuritates et spirituales intelligentias et utilitates auditoribus suisaperiunt , quasi numeros suos dividunt et. partiuulur. Et in calculo nomen norum scriptum , quod nemo scit, nisi qui accipit. Quod eat hocnomen Christi, quod in calculo Evangelii ,scriptum esse dicitur? In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat epud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum (Joan. I, 1) ; et iterum : Ego et Pater unum tumus (Joan. X, 30); etidem evangelista in alio lico dicit: Quia naM solum solvebat sabbutum, ted et Patremsuumdiscebat Deum, æqualem se faciens Deo (Joan. v, 18). Si Christus aequalem se faciebat Deo , cyr dicjt Arius minorem esse Filium Patre ? Iloc ergo nomen quod in calculo scriptum est, nullus scit, uisi qui accipit ; quia omnipotentiam , dwinitatem , æqualitatem Filii eumPatre nullus scire prevalet, nisi cui doctrina Evaugelii data fuerit.
passages.english: so the doctors of the Church gather many words of the Gospel in their hearts, and when they open up their obscurities, their spiritual meanings and their benefits to their hearers, they as it were divide and share out their numbers. "And on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it." What is this name of Christ which is said to be written on the stone of the Gospel? "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1); and again: "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30); and the same evangelist says in another place: "Because he was not only breaking the sabbath, but was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God" (John 5:18). If Christ made himself equal to God, why does Arius say that the Son is less than the Father? So this name which is written on the stone no one knows except the one who receives it; for no one is able to know the omnipotence, the divinity and the equality of the Son with the Father, except the one to whom the teaching of the Gospel has been given.
passages.notes: The text has many scanning errors, silently corrected (e.g. 'ill' for 'in', 'partiuulur' for 'partiuntur', 'norum' for 'novum', 'discebat' for 'dicebat', 'dwinitatem' for 'divinitatem'). 'Calculus' (here 'stone') means a small pebble used for counting; the context before plays on this sense.

passages.original: 12, 13.)Qui vicerit, faciam illum columnam in tent plo Dei mei, et forus nan egreditur amplius (.Galal. n, 2). Potest per templum Ecclesia designari: per co. lumnas autem, quæ sustentant templum, prædicatores. Nam et Paulus apostolus Petrum et Jacobum columnas Ecclesiae vocat; eo qundsuper ipsos ædificata sit. Ecclesia, sicut Dominus dixit Petro :Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam (Matth. XVI, 28). Sed videtur propter hoe, quod sequitur : Et foras non egredietur amptius; uon ad præsentem Ecclesiam, sed ad cœlestem pertinere hanc sententiam. Nam multi fuerunt, qui columnæ Ecclesiæ dicebantur : sed propter pravam doctrinam eorum , ab ea exierunt, sicut fuit Origenes, et alii mulli. Per templum ergo coelestis habitatio, per columnam vero unusquisque electus potest designari. Ergo qui vicerit omnia tentamenta diabolica , omnesque carnales vo. luptates, columna in templo Dci efficitur, id est, in cœlesti beatitudine : et sicut columna in loco, in quo statuitur, c firmissima stabilitate perseverat, ita et unusquisque electus in coelesti beatitudine tam firmissimam stabilitatem a creatore suo consequitur, ut numquam ab ea divellatur;
passages.english: 12, 13.) Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will go out no more (Gal. 2[:9]). By the temple the Church can be signified, and by the pillars which support the temple, the preachers. For the apostle Paul too calls Peter and James pillars of the Church, because the Church was built upon them, as the Lord said to Peter: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt. 16[:18]). But because of what follows, And he will go out no more, this statement seems to belong not to the present Church but to the heavenly one. For there were many who were called pillars of the Church, but because of their perverse teaching they went out from it, as Origen did, and many others. So by the temple the heavenly dwelling, and by the pillar each one of the elect, can be signified. Therefore whoever has conquered all the devil's temptations and all fleshly pleasures is made a pillar in the temple of God, that is, in heavenly blessedness; and just as a pillar remains with the firmest stability in the place where it is set up, so each one of the elect in heavenly blessedness obtains from his creator a stability so very firm that he is never torn away from it;
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-reference ('12, 13' continues 'Vers.' in the preceding context, i.e. Rev. 3:12). Scanning errors corrected: 'tent plo' = templo, 'forus nan egreditur' = foras non egredietur, 'qundsuper' = quod super, 'hoe' = hoc, 'amptius'/'uon' = amplius/non, 'Dci' = Dei; stray 'c' omitted. The printed citations 'Galal. n, 2' and 'Matth. XVI, 28' appear garbled; the references are Gal. 2:9 and Matt. 16:18.

passages.original: Per reges terræ principes et tribunos, eos qui hanc gentem regere videbantur, possumus intelligere : per divites et fortes, servos et liberos, cæteram multitudinem. Qualiter autem se in speluncis et petris montium absconderunt, Josephus manifeste narrat, qui eversionem Hierusalem describit (Joseph. lib. VI de bello Judaico c. ii et uq.). Tanta enim fuit afflictio, ut cum fame diutina consumerentur, et ab hostibus exterius, et multo deterius a prædonibus intrinsecus affligerentur;
passages.english: By the kings of the earth, the princes and tribunes, we can understand those who were seen to rule this nation; by the rich and the strong, slaves and free, the rest of the multitude. How they hid themselves in caves and in the rocks of the mountains Josephus relates plainly, who describes the overthrow of Jerusalem (Josephus, Jewish War book 6, ch. 2 and following). For the affliction was so great that, while they were being consumed by prolonged famine, and were afflicted by enemies from outside and, much worse, by brigands from within,
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete and continues in the following context. The citation 'c. ii et uq.' is read as 'c. 2 et seq.'

passages.original: quia Romanis datum eat a Deo, ut impios Judaeos diversis calamitatibus afflictos, quosdam occiderent, quosdam a sua terra evellerent. Et œstuaverunt hom magno. Quam magnus fuerit ille æstus, quo Romani Judæos arOixcruDL, qui vult scire, Josephum tegat, et inveniet nullam gentem in omnibus regnis terrarum atrocius periisse (De bello Judaico). Et blasphemaverunt nomen Dei habenli8 potestatem super has plagal. Tam impia fuit gens Judaeorum, ut cum scirent se pro sceleribus suis inaudita mala perpeti, non solum a blasphemiis Christi non cessaverint, sed etiam multo deteriores blasphemias in suis afflictionibus contra Deum evomuerint.
passages.english: because it was granted to the Romans by God that, once the impious Jews had been afflicted with various calamities, they should kill some and uproot others from their land. And men were scorched with great heat. How great that heat was with which the Romans [afflicted] the Jews, whoever wishes to know, let him read Josephus, and he will find that no nation in all the kingdoms of the earth perished more atrociously (Jewish War). And they blasphemed the name of God, who has power over these plagues. So impious was the nation of the Jews that, though they knew they were suffering unheard-of evils for their crimes, not only did they not cease from blaspheming Christ, but they even spewed out much worse blasphemies against God in their afflictions.
passages.notes: 'arOixcruDL' is corrupt; it presumably stands for a verb such as 'afflixerunt' (afflicted), and it is translated that way. Other scanning errors corrected: 'eat' = est, 'hom' = homines, 'tegat' = legat, 'habenli8' = habentis, 'plagal' = plagas.

passages.original: VII, 3), per quas quatuor regna figurabantur: quarta autem besua, quae erat fortis atque terribilis, perquam Romani designati sunt, decem cornua habuisse describitur, per quae ea regna quae Romanum imperium destruxerunt, designata sunt, sicut sanctus Hieronymus quorumdam assertionem sequens exponit (Comment. in cap. VII Daniel.). Eamdem itaque significationem habent decem cornua in hoc loco, quam et illa habuisse dicuntur; significant quippe ea regna, per quae Romanum imperium destructum est. Partem namque Asiae per se primi- tus abstulerunt : postea vero Saraceni totam sube- gerunt : Vandali Africam sibi vindicaverunt, Gothi Hispaniam , Longobardi Italiam , Burgundiones Galliam, Franci Germaniam, Hunni Pannoniam : Alani autem et Suevi multa loca depopulati sunt, quae eorum subjacebant ditioni.
passages.english: 7:3), by which four kingdoms were figured. The fourth beast, which was strong and terrible and by which the Romans were signified, is described as having had ten horns. By these were signified the kingdoms which destroyed the Roman empire, as Saint Jerome explains, following the assertion of certain people (Commentary on Daniel ch. 7). So the ten horns in this place have the same meaning that those are said to have had: they signify the kingdoms by which the Roman empire was destroyed. For [the Persians?] first took away part of Asia by themselves, but afterwards the Saracens subdued all of it; the Vandals claimed Africa for themselves, the Goths Spain, the Lombards Italy, the Burgundians Gaul, the Franks Germany, the Huns Pannonia; and the Alans and Suevi laid waste many places which lay under their rule.
passages.notes: 'Partem namque Asiae per se primitus abstulerunt' has no expressed subject; a people's name, probably the Persians, seems to have dropped out. 'Besua' is read as bestia (beast).

passages.original: Chrysoprasus lapis viridis aureique coloris esse perhibetur : qui pro eo quod in dccimo loco ponitur, possumus per eum quosdam doctores Ecclesiae intelligere, qui et verbis in corporibus positi multos docuerunt, et multo plures suis scriptis erudierunt d et erudiunt quotidie, ut fuerunt Hieronymus, Augustinus, Gregorius et multi alii; qui etiam et lumina Ecclesiæ recte dici possum: qui per viridem et aureum colorem designantur; eo quod viriditate fidei fuerint firmi, et sapientia, ut aurum fulgidi.
passages.english: The chrysoprase is said to be a stone of green and golden colour. Because it is placed in the tenth position, we can understand by it certain teachers of the Church who, while still living in their bodies, taught many by their words, and have instructed, and still instruct daily, many more by their writings, such as Jerome, Augustine, Gregory and many others. These can also rightly be called lights of the Church. They are signified by the green and golden colour because they were firm in the greenness of faith and shining like gold in wisdom.
passages.notes: Stray letter 'd' omitted; 'possum' is read as possunt (can).
